title: Space Shuttle (commander's station)

sources.title: NSTS 1988 News Reference: Rotational hand controllers (GlobalSecurity mirror)
JoyPro cockpit catalog (panels, items and grip functions of the variant)

intro: The Space Shuttle orbiter (1981-2011) was a reusable spaceplane: it launched like a rocket, flew in orbit like a spacecraft and glided home without engines to land on a runway. The commander sat on the left of the flight deck with a hand controller in front of the seat, the speed brake lever and a translation handle on the left, and rudder pedals. Controls and trim follow the NASA controllers workbook; panel numbers and button names follow the shuttle crew documents as known.

areas.name: Glareshield panel F2
areas.text: The flight control mode push buttons.

panels.name: Glareshield panel F2 (flight control mode PBIs)
panels.text: Lighted push buttons (PBIs) under the glareshield that decide whether the computers or the commander steer.
panels.context: During the return the commander often switched to CSS to fly the final approach and landing by hand.

controls.name: PITCH AUTO / CSS
controls.text: Push buttons that choose who steers the nose up and down: AUTO lets the guidance computers steer, CSS (control stick steering) lets the commander steer with the hand controller.
controls.context: The lit button shows which mode is active.

controls.name: ROLL/YAW AUTO / CSS
controls.text: The same choice for rolling and turning the orbiter: computers (AUTO) or the hand controller (CSS).
controls.context: Pitch and roll/yaw can be switched separately.

controls.name: SPD BK/THROT AUTO / MAN
controls.text: Buttons that choose whether the speed brake (and the engine throttle during launch) is set by the computers or by hand with the speed brake/thrust controller.
controls.context: The speed brake is a split rudder that opens to slow the orbiter during the glide home.

controls.name: BODY FLAP AUTO / MAN
controls.text: Buttons that choose whether the body flap, a movable plate under the engines, is moved by the computers or by hand.
controls.context: The body flap helps keep the nose at the right angle during the return through the atmosphere.

controls.name: Master alarm
controls.text: A light that comes on with a tone when a system has a problem. Pressing it switches the alarm off.
controls.context: The caution and warning matrix on the centre panel then shows which system it is.

areas.name: Forward panels F3, F6-F8
areas.text: Screens, abort switch, gear and drag chute.

panels.name: Forward panels F6-F8 (MEDS displays)
panels.text: The glass cockpit screens (MEDS) and the commander's flight panel F6 with the abort switch and the gear buttons.
panels.context: From 2000 the orbiters had these flat screens instead of the old round dials and tube screens.

controls.name: Commander's MDUs (CDR1, CDR2)
controls.text: The commander's two screens. They show the flight instruments (attitude, heading, speed and height tapes) or pages about the systems.
controls.context: The commander flies by them during launch and landing.

controls.name: Centre MDUs on F7
controls.text: The shared screens in the middle of the panel, which show the computer pages and system displays for both pilots.
controls.context: Commander and pilot work with them together.

controls.name: Caution and warning matrix (F7)
controls.text: A board of labelled lights, each saying which system has a problem.
controls.context: When the master alarm sounds, the crew looks here.

controls.name: Abort mode rotary switch and ABORT PBI (F6)

positions.name: TAL
positions.text: Land on a runway across the ocean.

positions.name: ATO
positions.text: Abort to a lower, safe orbit.

controls.text: A knob that chooses the kind of emergency return during launch, and a push button that starts it. RTLS turns back to the launch site, TAL lands across the ocean, ATO goes to a lower orbit.
controls.context: It was used once for real: in 1985 an engine failure led to an abort to orbit (ATO).

controls.name: Landing gear ARM and DN PBIs (F6)
controls.text: Two push buttons: ARM prepares the landing gear, DN lowers it.
controls.context: The gear goes down only shortly before touchdown, because it cannot be raised again in flight.

panels.name: Panel F3 (trim enable, drag chute)
panels.text: Switches between the two pilots' panels for enabling the trim and the buttons for the landing drag chute.
panels.context: They are used for the glide home and the landing.

controls.name: Trim RHC/PNL enable-inhibit
controls.text: This switch allows or blocks trimming with the hand controller and the panel trim switches.
controls.context: It is a safety switch that keeps the trim from being changed by accident.

controls.name: Trim panel on/off
controls.text: This switch powers the panel trim switches.
controls.context: Without power the panel trim switches do nothing.

controls.name: Drag chute ARM / DEPLOY / JETT PBIs
controls.text: Buttons for the drag chute, a big parachute behind the orbiter that helps it stop on the runway: arm it, let it out after touchdown, and throw it off when slow.
controls.context: It was added to the orbiters from 1992.

areas.name: Left panel L2
areas.text: Trim, body flap and entry mode.

panels.name: Left panel L2 (trim, body flap, entry mode)
panels.text: The commander's switches for the trim, the body flap and the entry flight control.
panels.context: They are used during the return and the glide to the runway.

controls.name: Panel trim switches
controls.text: Switches that trim the roll and yaw of the control surfaces (the movable parts of the wings and tail), small adjustments so the orbiter flies straight without holding the controls.
controls.context: They work only when the trim is enabled on panel F3.

controls.name: Body flap switch
controls.text: This switch moves the body flap up or down by hand.
controls.context: It is used when the body flap mode on F2 is set to manual.

controls.name: Entry mode switch

positions.name: NO Y JET
positions.text: The yaw jets are not used.

controls.text: This switch chooses how the flight control works during the return: normal, with lower gains, or without the yaw jets (the small rocket jets that turn the nose sideways).
controls.context: AUTO is the normal setting; the others are for failures.

areas.name: Centre console C3
areas.text: Orbital engines, flight control channels, autopilot.

panels.name: Centre console C3 (OMS, FCS channels)
panels.text: The console between the two seats with the orbital engine switches, the flight control channels, the autopilot buttons and the air data probes.
panels.context: Both pilots reach it; the autopilot buttons here were used throughout the time in orbit.

controls.name: OMS engine switches
controls.text: Switches that arm the two orbital manoeuvring engines (OMS), the engines at the tail that change the orbit and start the return.
controls.context: They are armed before every OMS burn, including the deorbit burn that brings the orbiter home.

controls.name: FCS channel switches

positions.name: OVERRIDE
positions.text: The channel is forced to stay on.

controls.text: Switches for the channels of the flight control system, the electronics that move the control surfaces. The channels back each other up.
controls.context: AUTO is normal; a bad channel can be switched off or forced on.

controls.name: DAP pushbuttons
controls.text: Buttons for the digital autopilot (DAP) in orbit: how the orbiter holds its attitude and how the hand controllers fire the steering jets.
controls.context: The crew set them for each task, for example docking or holding still for an experiment. JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

controls.name: Air data probe switches
controls.text: Switches that swing out the air data probes, small tubes on the nose that measure speed and height in the air.
controls.context: They are deployed during the glide home, once the orbiter is slow enough.

controls.name: Pilot's panel trim and body flap
controls.text: The second set of trim and body flap switches, for the pilot on the right.
controls.context: With them the pilot can trim and move the body flap just like the commander.

panels.name: Overhead panels O1-O17
panels.text: The panels in the roof with the computer switches and the circuit breakers.
panels.context: The five general purpose computers that fly the orbiter are switched here.

controls.name: GPC mode switches (O6)
controls.text: Switches for the general purpose computers (GPCs), the five computers that fly the orbiter. Each one can be stopped, put on standby or set to run.
controls.context: Four computers normally run the same program and vote; the fifth runs the backup flight system.

controls.name: Circuit breakers (O14-O16)
controls.text: Rows of circuit breakers, safety switches that cut the power to a system when it draws too much.
controls.context: The crew sets them with the checklists; a tripped breaker explains a dead system.

areas.name: Hand controllers and pedals
areas.text: Everything the commander holds or pushes.

panels.name: Rotational hand controller
panels.text: The pistol grip in front of the commander's seat, between the knees.
panels.context: It flies the orbiter by hand: through the steering jets in space and through the control surfaces in the air.

controls.name: Rotational hand controller (RHC)
controls.text: Moving the grip forward or back pitches the orbiter, sideways rolls it, twisting yaws it. Twisting for yaw works only during launch and in orbit; in the air the pedals turn the nose.
controls.context: On a joystick it is the X, Y and twist axes; the commander uses it for docking and for flying the landing by hand.

controls.name: RHC trim switch
controls.text: A four-way switch on top of the grip for the trim: forward and back trim the pitch, left and right the roll.
controls.context: Trim means small adjustments so the orbiter flies steadily without holding the grip. It works when the trim is enabled on panel F3.

controls.name: BFS engage button
controls.text: A red button on the grip that hands control to the backup flight system (BFS), the fifth computer with its own separately written program.
controls.context: It is the emergency step if the four main computers fail; it was never needed in flight.

controls.name: Communications switch
controls.text: While this switch on the grip is held, the commander's voice goes out on the radio or the intercom.
controls.context: It works like the button of a walkie-talkie.

panels.name: Speed brake/thrust controller (SBTC)
panels.text: The lever on the commander's left side console.
panels.context: On the commander's side it sets the speed brake during the glide home.

controls.name: Speed brake/thrust controller (SBTC), left
controls.text: Pulling this lever back opens the speed brake, the split rudder at the tail that opens like a book to slow the orbiter; pushing it forward closes it.
controls.context: The orbiter glides home without engine power, so the speed brake is the main way to control its speed.

controls.name: SBTC takeover switch
controls.text: Pressing this button on the lever hands the speed brake from the computers to the commander.
controls.context: From then on the lever sets the speed brake by hand.

panels.name: Translational hand controller
panels.text: The T-handle at the left of the commander's seat.
panels.context: It moves the orbiter in orbit without turning it; there is no use for it in the air.

controls.name: Translational hand controller (THC)
controls.text: This handle moves the whole orbiter without turning it (translation): forward, back, left, right, up and down, by firing the steering jets.
controls.context: It was used for meeting and docking with space stations and for catching satellites; on a joystick it is a second three-axis controller.

panels.name: Rudder pedals
panels.text: The pedals at the commander's feet with toe brakes on top.
panels.context: They work in the air and on the runway, not in space.

controls.name: Rudder pedals (RPTA)
controls.text: Pushing the left or right pedal moves the rudder at the tail and, on the runway, steers the nose wheel.
controls.context: They are used in the last part of the glide and to keep the orbiter on the runway centre line.

controls.name: Left toe brake
controls.text: Pressing the top of the left pedal brakes the left main wheels.
controls.context: The commander brakes after the nose wheel is down; braking one side more helps steer.

controls.name: Right toe brake
controls.text: Pressing the top of the right pedal brakes the right main wheels.
controls.context: It is used together with the left toe brake to stop on the runway.
